argument: This first episode on Simone Weil introduces her as a philosopher who lived her ideas rather than merely writing about them, and it centers her lifelong preoccupation with attention: the way we orient ourselves toward experience determines not just the quality but the very possibility of what we can experience. Weil criticized how school conditions people to search for a single correct answer rather than stay open to reality, and how factory work and other forms of 'affliction' strip people of the ability to think. Her alternative was a receptive, expectation-free kind of attention that can transform both how we learn and how we treat other people.
keyIdeas: Weil is presented as a 'living philosopher' — someone whose insights are inseparable from the extreme, embodied choices she made (fighting in the Spanish Civil War, working in a factory), unlike academic philosophers who theorize from a safe distance.

Attention, for Weil, is not just about the quality of experience — it determines which experiences are even possible for a person to have at all, like tuning into a radio frequency that was always broadcasting.

Her teaching method (letting students seek out new problems rather than search for fixed answers) reflects her belief that training people to hunt for 'the answer' limits their capacity for open thought on harder, non-mathematical questions.

'Negative activity' is a third path between passive inaction and forceful willed effort — it means doing the work of removing your own baggage, prejudices, and expectations so a different reality can disclose itself to you.

Working in a factory taught Weil that thinking is the first thing sacrificed for survival under a production quota, and that this same dynamic — being turned into a controllable thing incapable of thinking your way out — defines 'Affliction' wherever it appears, from soldiers to factory workers.

terms.def: Weil's central concept: an open, receptive orientation toward reality that determines what experiences are available to a person, as opposed to searching or forcing.
A middle path between doing nothing and forcing a solution through effort — putting in effort to remove one's own baggage and expectations rather than to add force.
Weil's term for the state produced when people are turned from human beings into things, grouped into controllable collectives, and rendered incapable of thinking their way out.
Weil's organizing concept for how human events move, analogous to how gravity governs physical events; underlies the domination of people as means to others' ends.
